title: Councils continue
hook: since Vatican II, bishops meet in synods, including recent ones where laypeople also voted

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nostra Aetate. Your line was no one may be forced. That was the last of the council's documents on this path. Today, the last day of the councils, and what came after.

Round tables in a big hall in Rome. At each one, a handful of people: a cardinal, a parish priest, a sister, a young mother, a theology professor. They take turns speaking, and the rule is that each person finishes before anyone answers. Then there's silence, and prayer, and another round. It looks less like a parliament than a long family dinner. This is what a gathering of the Church can look like now, and it has an old Greek name: synod.
screen: `ROUND TABLES IN ROME.` → `EACH ONE FINISHES SPEAKING.` → `SYNOD.`

segments.voice: Synod is a Greek word for a meeting or assembly of the Church. Pope Francis has explained it simply: walking together. Here's how the habit grew. First, the council itself. Bishops at Vatican Two wanted bishops from around the world to help the pope in caring for the whole Church. While the council was still meeting, Pope Paul the Sixth set up the Synod of Bishops, a gathering that meets again and again in Rome, between councils, on questions like the family, young people, or the Word of God. Second, the widening. In recent synods, laypeople, women and men, sat at the tables, and some of them voted alongside the bishops. Before the meetings, parishes around the world were asked to listen to their own people and send up what they heard. Third, the method. Pope Francis has described a synodal Church as one that listens, where each person has something to learn from the others. Catholics differ about how far this should go and what it should decide; that argument is itself part of the walk. Fourth, the oldest picture. On the road to Emmaus, two disciples were walking and reasoning together, and in the Douay-Rheims, "Jesus himself also drawing near, went with them." He listened first, and asked them what they were talking about. Over the last thirty days this path has walked from Nicaea through Ephesus and Chalcedon, to Trent and both Vatican councils. The meetings never really stopped.
screen: `SYNOD: AN ASSEMBLY.` · `THE SYNOD OF BISHOPS.` · `LAYPEOPLE AT THE TABLE.` · `A CHURCH THAT LISTENS.` · then, large: `WALKING TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Recall the last conversation where you were already composing your answer while the other person talked, and replay it slowly, this time hearing them out to the end of every sentence. Saint James put it this way: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak." If you pray, ask for that patience.
Synod. A gathering of the Church, which Pope Francis calls walking together; since the council, bishops and now laypeople meet in synods. Today's word.
Your line: walking together. Tomorrow, a new block: the middle ages, beginning inside a monastery. Rest well.

chat.says: What actually happens at a synod in Rome?
options: People gather at tables; each speaks and is heard out, then silence, prayer, another round.
Bishops debate in a chamber, and a majority vote decides new doctrine for all.
Cardinals meet in secret, mainly to elect the next pope when the seat is empty.

notes: Last day of Block B (councils, days 767–796); the teach names the block's journey briefly ('the last thirty days' counts the path's own days, not a historical claim). Next block (797–846) is the middle ages.
The Greek 'synodos' (syn + hodos, with + way) is a standard lexicon derivation (LSJ); Pope Francis's 'walking together' is paraphrased. Confirm under the etymology rule.
Hook's round-table description reflects the recent synod's 'conversation in the Spirit' format; confirm details (taking turns, silence, prayer) and that laypeople voted.
'Some of them voted alongside the bishops' — confirm wording; the index hook supplies the claim.
Christus Dominus 5 and Apostolica Sollicitudo paraphrased. Confirm.
Luke 24:15 and James 1:19 Douay-Rheims fragments — confirm exact wording.
Review says Nostra Aetate/Dignitatis Humanae was 'the last of the council's documents on this path' (i.e. in this course); confirm against the outline.
Editor: cut the syn + hodos etymology from teach, word, original note and trapdoor (claims rule: no cited text gives it); 'walking together' is now attributed to Pope Francis only.
Editor (second pass): the teach's first screen head ('synod: a way, together') still implied the cut syn + hodos etymology; now 'synod: an assembly'. The earlier note on LSJ is superseded.

Audit (2026-10-01): sequencing fixed. Apostolica Sollicitudo (Sept. 1965) came before Christus Dominus was promulgated (Oct. 1965), so the Synod did not 'answer' the decree; voice now says bishops at the council wanted it and Paul VI set it up while the council was still meeting. Emmaus 'arguing' changed to 'reasoning together' to match the Douay-Rheims 'talked and reasoned' (Luke 24:15).
